questions.explanation: `std::array` is a value type that wraps `double[3]`. Passing it by value **copies** all 24 bytes, so `v` is unchanged. It never decays to a pointer, so `sizeof` is 3×8 = 24. A raw `double v[3]` parameter decays to `double*`, and there the write *would* hit the caller's data.

options: 0; a[3] is indeterminate (reading it is UB)
questions.explanation: `std::array` is an aggregate with no constructor. A default-initialised local leaves `int`s indeterminate, just like a C array. `{}` value-initialises everything to 0. Always write `std::array<double,3> v{};`.

questions.prompt: Which is true about `std::deque<ImuSample> d` after `d.push_back(s)`?
options: All iterators AND references are invalidated
Iterators are invalidated, but references/pointers to existing elements stay valid
Only `end()` is invalidated, like vector without reallocation
questions.explanation: A deque is a map of fixed-size blocks. Pushing at either end may reallocate the *map* (so iterators break) but never moves existing elements (so references survive). Inserting in the **middle** invalidates both. `pop_front`/`pop_back` invalidate only the erased element (plus end()).

questions.prompt: You need a FIFO of the last 2 s of IMU samples: push at the back, pop at the front, occasional random access. Best default?
questions.explanation: `deque` has O(1) at both ends plus random access, and decent locality (contiguous blocks). `vector::erase(begin())` is O(n). `std::list` costs one heap allocation and two pointers per node and has terrible cache behaviour. A fixed-capacity ring buffer is the other common answer.

`auto [id, w] = p;` binds names to a hidden **copy** of `p`, so `w = 9` doesn't touch `p`. `auto& [rid, rw] = p;` binds to `p` itself, so `rw = 7` changes `p.second`. The same rule applies in loops: `for (auto& [k, v] : map)`.

questions.prompt: When is `std::list` genuinely the right choice?
options: When you need stable iterators/references and O(1) splice/insert/erase at known positions (e.g. an LRU cache list)
questions.explanation: `list` wins only when **iterator stability** and O(1) splice matter: an LRU list paired with an `unordered_map` of iterators, for example. For bulk insertion, `vector` usually wins anyway because of cache locality, even with O(n) shifts.

questions.explanation: `std::get<2>` is the string "imu" (size 3). `tuple_size_v` is 3. Indices to `std::get` must be compile-time constants. `std::get<std::string>(t)` also works because the type is unique in the tuple.

options: true, because comparison is lexicographic: first 1 < 2 decides
questions.explanation: `pair` and `tuple` compare **lexicographically**: first by `.first`, then by `.second` only on a tie. That's why `(timestamp, id)` tuples sort by time and break ties by id, and why `std::tie(a.t, a.id) < std::tie(b.t, b.id)` is the idiomatic way to write a comparator.
